title: Waiting properly: semaphores and condition variables
objective: By the end of this lesson you can make a thread wait for a condition without burning CPU, explain why the wait must sit in a while loop rather than an if, and choose between a semaphore and a condition variable.

blocks.text: A mutex answers 'only one at a time'. It does not answer 'wait until there is something to do'. For that you need a thread to sleep until another thread tells it the world has changed — and the naive version of that is one of the most wasteful things you can write.

blocks.caption: The wrong way, and why it is wrong
lines: /* Busy waiting: burns a core doing nothing */
usleep(1000);      /* now it is slow AND still wasteful */
/* Adds up to 1 ms of latency to every item, and still wakes 1000x/second */

blocks.text: A condition variable: sleep until told

pthread_cond_wait does something that looks impossible at first: it releases the mutex and goes to sleep as one indivisible step, and re-acquires the mutex before returning. That atomicity is the entire point — without it, a signal arriving between 'release' and 'sleep' would be missed, and the thread would sleep forever.

blocks.caption: The pattern — memorise this shape
lines: while (items == 0) {                 /* WHILE, never if — see below */
pthread_cond_wait(&cv, &m);      /* unlock + sleep atomically; relock on wake */

blocks.text: This is the single most common bug in code that uses condition variables, and it is easy to demonstrate. Three consumers wait; the producer adds one item and calls broadcast, waking all three. With while, each re-checks the condition, two find nothing and go back to sleep, and the count ends at zero. With if, each assumes the condition must be true because it was woken.

blocks.caption: Measured, on the same program with one line changed
lines: result: items=0, consumers that took a nonexistent item: 0
consumer 1 took an item that was NOT there (items=0)
consumer 2 took an item that was NOT there (items=-1)
result: items=-2, consumers that took a nonexistent item: 2

blocks.title: Three separate reasons the condition can be false after a wake
blocks.text: First, broadcast wakes every waiter but the resource may only satisfy one — demonstrated above. Second, another thread can take the item between your wake-up and your re-acquiring the mutex. Third, the standard explicitly permits spurious wake-ups: a wait may return with nothing having happened at all. Any one of these is enough; together they make while mandatory. Treat a wake-up as 'go and check', never as 'it is your turn'.

rows: One item became available and any waiter can take it
State changed in a way different waiters judge differently
Waking a waiter that cannot proceed while another could
A thundering herd: all wake, one proceeds, the rest sleep again

blocks.text: A semaphore: a counter you can wait on

blocks.caption: Simpler, when counting is all you need
lines: sem_init(&slots, 0, 5);      /* 5 permits: at most 5 threads inside */
sem_wait(&slots);            /* take one; sleep if the count is 0 */
sem_post(&slots);            /* give it back; wakes a waiter if any */

headers: Reach for a condition variable when
rows: The condition is 'how many are available'
The condition is arbitrary — a predicate over your own state
Waiting for 'the queue is non-empty and not shutting down'
No shared data needs protecting alongside
You already hold a mutex over the data

blocks.title: A semaphore remembers; a condition variable does not
blocks.text: sem_post on a semaphore nobody is waiting on increments the count, and a later sem_wait returns immediately. pthread_cond_signal with no waiter is simply lost — nothing records that it happened. That is precisely why the condition variable pattern keeps its own state variable and re-checks it: the state, not the signal, is the source of truth.

blocks.title: Build the bug and remove it
steps: Write a program with three consumer threads waiting on a condition variable for items > 0
Have the main thread set items = 1 and call pthread_cond_broadcast
Run it with the wait inside a while loop and print the final count
Change while to if, run again, and print the count — expect it to go negative
Explain out loud which of the three reasons above caused it here
Now replace the whole thing with a semaphore initialised to 0: sem_post once, and confirm exactly one consumer proceeds
Add a shutdown flag and make the wait condition (items > 0 || shutting_down) — this is the form a real server needs
Run the while version under -fsanitize=thread and confirm it is clean
blocks.expected: A count that goes negative with if and stays correct with while, from a one-word change. The last two steps matter for the capstone: a wait condition that only covers the happy path leaves your threads asleep forever when the program tries to shut down.

cheatsheet: Busy waiting burns a core; sleeping-and-polling adds latency and still wastes wakeups
pthread_cond_wait releases the mutex and sleeps atomically, then re-acquires it
ALWAYS wait in a while loop that re-checks the condition, never an if
Three reasons the condition can be false on wake: broadcast, another thread took it, spurious wakeups
Measured: with if, three consumers over one item drove the count to -2
signal wakes one waiter; broadcast wakes all
A semaphore counts and remembers; a condition variable signal with no waiter is lost
Semaphore for 'how many available'; condition variable for an arbitrary predicate
Include shutdown in the wait condition, or threads sleep forever at exit

checkpoint.prompt: Why must pthread_cond_wait release the mutex and sleep as one indivisible step?

choices.A: To avoid deadlock with the scheduler
choices.B: Otherwise a signal arriving between releasing and sleeping would be missed, and the thread would sleep forever
choices.D: To let the compiler optimise the loop

checkpoint.explanation: That gap is exactly the race the atomic release-and-sleep exists to close. It is also why you must hold the mutex when you call it.

checkpoint.prompt: Three threads wait on a condition variable. The producer adds one item and calls broadcast. With if instead of while, what happens?

choices.A: Only one proceeds; the others go back to sleep
choices.B: All three proceed as if an item were available, and the count goes negative
choices.D: broadcast blocks until all three are served

checkpoint.explanation: Verified: the count reached -2 in exactly this experiment. Waking up means 'go and check', not 'the condition holds'.

checkpoint.prompt: A thread calls pthread_cond_signal while nobody is waiting. What happens to that signal?

choices.A: It is queued for the next waiter
choices.B: It is lost — condition variables keep no state, which is why the pattern re-checks a state variable
choices.D: It wakes the next thread that waits, within one second

checkpoint.explanation: A semaphore would have remembered it by incrementing its count. This difference is usually what decides which one to use.

checkpoint.prompt: Your worker threads wait for (queue_not_empty). At shutdown the program hangs. Why?

choices.B: Nothing ever makes the wait condition true again, so the workers sleep forever — the condition must also cover shutting down

checkpoint.explanation: A wait condition that only describes the happy path has no exit. Make it (queue_not_empty || shutting_down), set the flag, and broadcast.
